explanations.explanation: That's the word, baker. On hearing it, many of His disciples said, “This is a difficult teaching. Who can accept it?” That's a lot like me staring at a new recipe and announcing, "Who can accept this much dough?"

Not quite, friend. On hearing it, many of His disciples said, “This is a difficult teaching. Who can accept it?” They call it difficult, not familiar. In their own words, it's a hard teaching to accept.
I love a good compliment, but that's not what they say. The text has them saying, “This is a difficult teaching. Who can accept it?” They call it difficult, and they ask who can accept it.
I see why you'd think so, but the text says Jesus was “Aware that His disciples were grumbling about this teaching…” So He knew. That makes the statement false. Their grumbling didn't get past Him.
That's right. John 6:61 says Jesus was “Aware that His disciples were grumbling about this teaching…” They're grumbling, and He knows it. Then He asks them, “Does this offend you?”

That's it, baker. Jesus says, "The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing." Then He adds, "The words I have spoken to you are spirit and they are life." Life comes from the Spirit, and that's what He wants them to hear.

I get why the Law comes to mind, since it's a big word in the Bible. But Jesus doesn't say it here. He says, "The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing." The Spirit is the one He names as giving life.
Good guess for a holy place, but the temple isn't in this sentence at all. Jesus says, “The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing.” He names the Spirit as the One who gives life.

Yes, and the writer adds it right into the story: “For Jesus had known from the beginning which of them did not believe and who would betray Him.” So when Jesus says some of them don't believe, He isn't finding out right then. He already knew.

Not quite, friend. The writer steps in with a note: "For Jesus had known from the beginning which of them did not believe and who would betray Him." The words "…from the beginning…" settle it. This was no surprise to Jesus.

explanations.answer: The Father has granted it to him
explanations.explanation: That's what He says. "This is why I told you that no one can come to Me unless the Father has granted it to him." Jesus is pointing back to something He'd said earlier. It's a heavy line, so let it sit a minute.

explanations.answer: He keeps every law of Moses
explanations.explanation: That's a very reasonable thing to guess, but it's not in this verse. Jesus says, "…no one can come to Me unless the Father has granted it to him." The Father granting it is the whole answer here. Nobody gets a gold star on a keeping-the-rules chart.

explanations.answer: He was born a son of Abraham
explanations.explanation: Abraham is a big name in the Bible, but he isn't mentioned in this passage. Jesus says, "…no one can come to Me unless the Father has granted it to him." So it comes down to what the Father grants, not to a family tree.

explanations.answer: Turn back and stop walking with Him
explanations.explanation: That's what happens. "From that time on many of His disciples turned back and no longer walked with Him." It's a heavy part of the story, and I think it's okay to just say so. They didn't wander off by accident, they turned around.

explanations.answer: Stay and ask Him to explain it
explanations.explanation: That would be a nice ending, and honestly I'd have loved it. But the text says, “From that time on many of His disciples turned back and no longer walked with Him.” They turned back, and I think that's a sad turn in the story.

explanations.answer: Go back to the synagogue to argue
explanations.explanation: Arguing isn't mentioned here. The text says, “…many of His disciples turned back and no longer walked with Him.” They stopped walking with Him, and that's all we're told. No synagogue and no arguing are in that verse.
You got it. Jesus turns to the Twelve and asks, “Do you want to leave too?” Many disciples have just turned back (John 6:66), and now He puts the question straight to the Twelve.
I see why a bigger group comes to mind, but the text says, “So Jesus asked the Twelve…” He asks the Twelve. That's who the question goes to.
The Pharisees aren't named anywhere in this passage. John 6:67 says, “So Jesus asked the Twelve…” So the question goes to the Twelve. I'd have asked the folks closest to me too.

explanations.answer: Jesus has the words of eternal life
explanations.explanation: That's what Simon Peter, one of the Twelve, says. "Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life." He doesn't list a bunch of reasons. He gives one, and it's the best one.

explanations.answer: Jesus fed thousands with five loaves
explanations.explanation: That did happen earlier in this chapter (John 6:9-13), and it's a great story. But it isn't the reason Peter gives. Simon Peter, one of the Twelve, says, "You have the words of eternal life." His answer is about Jesus' words.

explanations.answer: Jesus healed so many of the sick
explanations.explanation: That's a kind thing to point to, but it isn't what Peter says. Simon Peter, one of the Twelve, says, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life.” That's his whole reason, and it's all about what Jesus says.

explanations.answer: He is the Holy One of God
explanations.explanation: Right on. Peter says, “We believe and know that You are the Holy One of God.” He says it straight to Jesus. And notice he says both believe and know.

explanations.answer: He is a prophet like Moses
explanations.explanation: Peter doesn't compare Jesus to anybody here. What he says is, “We believe and know that You are the Holy One of God.” He says it plain.

explanations.answer: He is a teacher from Capernaum
explanations.explanation: Peter isn't describing a teacher at all. He says something much bigger: “We believe and know that You are the Holy One of God.” He's saying who Jesus is.

Yes, He says it right after the question. "Have I not chosen you, the Twelve? Yet one of you is a devil!" It's a sobering moment, and I think it's okay to just let it be heavy. Right after Peter's strong answer, Jesus says something hard.

I know it's a hard one to believe, but He does say it. The text has Jesus answer, "Have I not chosen you, the Twelve? Yet one of you is a devil!" So the statement is true. Verse 71 goes on to tell us who He meant.

That's who the writer names. "He was speaking about Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot." The writer doesn't leave us guessing. I think it's a hard thing to read, because Judas was in the group of the Twelve.

Thomas is one of the Twelve (John 20:24), but he isn't the name here. The writer says, "He was speaking about Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot." So it's Judas, and John 6:71 spells it out. No need to go hunting through the list.
Matthew, the tax collector, is one of the Twelve too (Matthew 10:3). But he isn't who the writer names. John 6:71 says, "He was speaking about Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot." So it's Judas.

That's the word. "For although Judas was one of the Twelve, he was later to betray Jesus." He was in the group, and the writer tells us what he'd do later. It's a heavy way to end this part of the story.
Not quite, friend. That isn't the word the writer uses. John 6:71 says, “…he was later to betray Jesus.” Betray is the word for Judas here. I'd keep that one in your pocket.

I wish that were the ending, I really do. But the text says the opposite: "…he was later to betray Jesus." Judas was one of the Twelve, and that's what he was going to do. It's a sad line, and I think it's okay to say so.
